## Setup

### Start a VSCode service

- [ ] Connect to the [SSP Cloud](https://www.sspcloud.fr/){target="_blank"}
- [ ] Start a `Vscode-python` service, then open it

### Retrieve the code

There are two possibilities to retrieve the code:

- clone the teacher's repository directly
  - `git clone https://github.com/ludo2ne/ENSAI-2A-remise-a-niveau.git`
- create a fork of this repository, then clone this fork
  - https://github.com/ludo2ne/ENSAI-2A-remise-a-niveau/fork{target="_blank"}
  - `git clone https://$GIT_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN@github.com/<username>/ENSAI-2A-remise-a-niveau.git`

If you clone the teacher's repository directly, you will not be able to use Git to keep track of your work. You will have to download the files manually, for example.

A fork is a copy of a remote repository. Since this copy belongs to you, you have the right to modify the code.

- [ ] Clone the repository by choosing one of the two options above

Then, go to the `src/POO` folder:

- [ ] File > Open Folder > `/home/onyxia/work/ENSAI-2A-remise-a-niveau/src/Python-POO/`
  - or directly from the terminal: `code-server /home/onyxia/work/ENSAI-2A-remise-a-niveau/src/Python-POO/`

You can then code in the files in the *exercise* folder. If needed, you can create new files.

## Exercise 1 - Points

Define a `Point` class to represent a point in the plane with x and y coordinates.

Implement the following methods:

- [ ] `__init__(self, x, y)`: point constructor with Cartesian coordinates
- [ ] `r(self)` and `t(self)`: returning the polar coordinates of the point
- [ ] `__str__(self)`: to display the Point as text, e.g. `(1.0, 2.4)`
- [ ] `distance(self, other_point)`: distance to another point
- [ ] `__eq__(self, other_point) -> bool`: indicates whether the two points are identical
- [ ] `homothety(self, k)`: applying a homothety centered at (0, 0) with ratio k
- [ ] `translation(self, dx, dy)`: applying a translation with vector (dx, dy)
- [ ] `rotation(self, a)` (bonus): applying a rotation centered at (0, 0) with angle a

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
To check that your methods are correct, you can add a `main` block at the end of your class. When you execute this file, this code will be run.

```{.python}
class Point:

    # ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    p1 = Point(1, 2)
    p2 = Point(1, 2)
    print(f"p1 : {p1}")
    print(f"Distance between p1 and p2 : {p1.distance(p2)}")
    print(f"p1 is equal to p2 : {p1 == p2}")
```

:::

## Exercise 2 - Polygons

* [ ] Create a `Polygon` class composed of objects from the `Point` class
  * We will assume from now on that segments do not cross
* [ ] Add 2 abstract methods `area()` and `perimeter()` to this class
  * these methods will be defined in child classes
* [ ] Create the `Segment`, `Triangle` and `Quadrilateral` classes that inherit from the `Polygon` class
  * check the number of points each time
* [ ] Define the `area()` and `perimeter()` methods in these 3 classes
* [ ] Create the `Rectangle` class that inherits from `Quadrilateral`
* [ ] For Rectangle, check that the 2 opposite sides have the same length and that there is a right angle

Here is the class diagram generated with [Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org/syntax/classDiagram.html){target="_blank"}

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    Point --o Polygon
    Polygon <|-- Segment : 2
    Polygon <|-- Triangle : 3
    Polygon <|-- Quadrilateral : 4
    Quadrilateral <|-- Rectangle
    class Point{
        +float x
        +float y
        +distance(other_point)
    }
    class Polygon{
        +list[Point] points_list
        +area()
        +perimeter()
    }
    class Quadrilateral{
        +area()
        +perimeter()
    }
    class Segment{
        +area()
        +perimeter()
    }
    class Triangle{
        +area()
        +perimeter()
    }
```

## Exercise 3 - Domino

### A Domino

Write a `Domino` class with:

* [ ] 2 integer attributes between 0 and 6: `end_A` and `end_B`
* [ ] `__str__()`: which displays the dots present on both ends
* [ ] `flip()`: which flips the domino (its A end becomes its B end and vice versa)
* [ ] `accepts_after(other_domino)`: checks whether the B end of the current domino has the same value as the A end of the other domino

### Game

Now we will try to code a domino game.

For simplicity:

* there will only be one player
* it is only possible to place a domino on one side, at the end of the domino row

Let's start by generating all possible dominoes, i.e. all combinations from (0,0) to (6,6) without duplicates.

* [ ] Write a function that generates all dominoes and returns the list
* [ ] Write an `display_dominoes()` function that displays a list of dominoes
* [ ] Write a `draw()` function that randomly draws a domino from a list and removes it from that list
* [ ] Write a `playable_dominoes(hand_dominoes, placed_dominoes)` function that takes two lists of dominoes as arguments. The function returns the list of dominoes in hand that could be placed after the last domino in the `placed_dominoes` list.

Write a `play()` function that:

* [ ] generates the list of all dominoes
* [ ] randomly draws a first domino and places it in the `placed_dominoes` list
* [ ] randomly distributes 6 dominoes to the player
* [ ] displays the dominoes they can play
* [ ] if no domino can be played, offer them the possibility to draw
* [ ] asks which domino they want to play (for example by asking them to enter the number in the domino list, and `quit` to stop playing)
* [ ] adds the played domino to the `placed_dominoes` list and removes it from the `hand_dominoes` list

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    class Domino{
        +int end_A
        +int end_B
        +flip()
        +accepts_after(other_domino)
    }
```
